title: Regional Cinema Dominates IFFM 2026 as Indian Film Breaks Free of Bollywood's Shadow
excerpt: Kannada, Malayalam, and Assamese films swept major awards at the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne, underscoring how Indian cinema's center of gravity is shifting beyond Hindi.
body:
• Malayalam film "Lokah Chapter 1: Chandra" won Best Film at IFFM 2026, while Kannada filmmaker Rishab Shetty took Best Director for "Kantara: A Legend Chapter 1"
  • Dulquer Salmaan, who rose from Malayalam cinema, won Best Actor for "Kaantha," reflecting the growing pan-Indian mobility of regional talent
  • The inaugural INCA Awards in April 2026 recognized excellence across 12 Indian language industries for the first time under one platform
  • Regional-language films now outnumber Bollywood and Hollywood combined on Indian ticketing platforms, signaling a structural shift in audience preferences

Melbourne's Message to Mumbai

https://youtube.com/watch?v=8MAW3IaCO60

The 17th edition of the Indian Film Festival of Melbourne delivered a verdict that would have been unthinkable a decade ago: not a single Hindi-language film took home a top competitive award. Malayalam cinema's "Lokah Chapter 1: Chandra" won Best Film. Kannada filmmaker Rishab Shetty claimed Best Director for "Kantara: A Legend Chapter 1." Assamese director Rima Das took Best Indie Film for "Not a Hero."

The results at IFFM 2026, Australia's largest celebration of Indian cinema outside India, aren't an anomaly. They reflect a tectonic shift in the Indian film landscape, where stories rooted in regional cultures, languages, and folklore are commanding national and international attention in ways that Bollywood's Hindi-language establishment never anticipated.

"Storytelling has always been my way of celebrating our culture, our traditions and the communities that inspire us. It is incredibly meaningful to see stories rooted in our heritage resonate with audiences across the world."

— Rishab Shetty, Best Director, IFFM 2026

The Numbers Tell the Story

A glance at BookMyShow, India's dominant ticketing platform, confirms what festival circuits have been signaling for years: regional-language films in Tamil, Telugu, Malayalam, Marathi, and Bhojpuri now outnumber Bollywood and Hollywood screenings combined. The audience has voted with its wallet, and the future, as the British Film Institute noted, is "glocal — you can be universal by being local."

Dulquer Salmaan's Best Actor win for "Kaantha" embodies this shift. The actor rose through Malayalam cinema before becoming a pan-Indian phenomenon, working across languages without relocating to Mumbai or conforming to Bollywood's star-making machinery. His trajectory mirrors that of other regional actors — from Telugu star Ram Charan to Tamil's Vijay — who have built massive followings without the traditional Hindi-film launch pad.

A New Infrastructure for Recognition

India's film industry is also building institutions to match its evolving landscape. The inaugural Indian National Cine Academy (INCA) Awards, held in Mumbai in April 2026, recognized Best Film, Best Actor, and Best Actress in each of 12 Indian languages — from Hindi and Tamil to Bhojpuri, Assamese, and Odia — under a single unified platform for the first time.

The 70th Filmfare Awards South, held in Kochi in February 2026, highlighted the depth of talent in South Indian cinema. Malayalam film "Aadujeevitham" led with eight nominations. The National Indian Film Festival of Australia (NIFFA), in its 2026 edition, presented awards to Kannada, Marathi, and documentary films alongside special honours for Anupam Kher and filmmaker Anubhav Sinha.

These platforms represent a departure from the old model where national film awards were the only venue for cross-linguistic recognition, and where Hindi cinema invariably dominated the conversation.

What's Driving the Shift

Several forces are converging. Streaming platforms like Netflix, Amazon Prime Video, and JioCinema have given regional films distribution reach that previously required theatrical runs in unfamiliar markets. A generation of smartphone users — India now has over 700 million — consumes content in their mother tongue rather than defaulting to Hindi.

At IFFM 2026, the festival brought together artists spanning generations: veteran actress Rekha received the Excellence in Cinema award, while Pankaj Tripathi was honored as Artist of Distinction. Rani Mukerji received recognition for 30 years in cinema. The breadth of honorees — from Bollywood veterans to regional disruptors — suggests the industry isn't splitting apart but rather expanding its definition of what counts as Indian cinema.

For the Indian diaspora, particularly in markets like Australia, the UK, and North America, this diversification means more of their specific linguistic and cultural identities are reflected on screen. A Malayali family in Melbourne can see their stories win Best Film at their city's own festival. That visibility matters.

nri_angle: IFFM, held in Melbourne with state government backing, is the largest celebration of Indian cinema outside India and serves as a cultural bridge for the Australian-Indian diaspora, showcasing stories in languages that reflect their diverse regional roots.
author: Diaspora Desk
